title: Factory Method: create different Vehicle types, different Payment methods.
shortTitle: Design using the Factory Method pattern
keyPoints: Factory Method centralises object creation so callers ask for a type and receive the right concrete instance without naming the concrete class.
The structure has a product interface, concrete products, and a factory with a creation method that takes a type parameter and returns the product.
Callers depend only on the product interface, satisfying Dependency Inversion and Open/Closed principles.
Adding a new product type means writing one new class and one case in the factory with zero changes to existing callers.
The simple parameterised factory is the most common interview and production form, distinct from the formal Factory Method and Abstract Factory.
Creation logic, dependency wiring, and configuration reading are hidden inside the factory instead of duplicated at every call site.

s1_definition.oneliner: The Factory Method centralises object creation so callers ask for a type and receive the right concrete instance without naming the concrete class.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Factory Method** – a creational pattern that defines an interface for creating an object but lets a dedicated factory decide which concrete class to instantiate based on input.
- **Product interface** – the common type returned by the factory, for example `PaymentMethod`, so callers depend only on this abstraction.
- **Concrete products** – specific implementations like `UpiPayment`, `CardPayment`, and `NetBankingPayment` that the factory selects at runtime.
- **Parameterised factory** – the most common form, where a static `create(String type)` method uses a type code to pick the right product.
- **Decoupling** – callers never use `new` on concrete classes, so adding a new product requires zero changes to existing caller code.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the account-opening desk at National Bank of India. Rajesh does not personally construct a savings account object; he tells the desk "savings" and the desk produces the right kind of account. If Priya asks for a current account, the same desk builds that instead. The caller names what they want; the factory knows how to construct it. The desk is the factory, the request type is the parameter, and the account handed back is the product.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Client Code
       │
       │  PaymentFactory.create("UPI")
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          PaymentFactory              │
  │                                      │
  │  "UPI"  ──→  new UpiPayment()        │
  │  "CARD" ──→  new CardPayment()       │
  │  "NET"  ──→  new NetBankingPayment() │
  └─────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                │
                │  returns PaymentMethod
                ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │     <<interface>> PaymentMethod      │
  │  + pay(accountId, amount)            │
  │  + type()                            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
         ▲            ▲            ▲
         │            │            │
   UpiPayment   CardPayment  NetBankingPayment
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Factory Method pattern defines a single place responsible for creating objects, so that callers ask for a type and receive the right concrete instance without ever naming the concrete class themselves. At National Bank of India, Rajesh uses it for payment methods and account types, where the calling code should say UPI or savings and not care how that object is wired together.

The structure is a product interface, several concrete products that implement it, and a factory whose creation method takes a type and returns the product. Because callers depend only on the interface, the pattern satisfies Dependency Inversion. Because adding a new payment method is just a new product class plus one case in the factory, it satisfies Open/Closed. The calling code that processes payments never changes.

The real-world benefit is that creation logic lives in exactly one place. When building a payment method involves reading configuration, wiring dependencies, or applying caching, that complexity is hidden inside the factory instead of being copy-pasted at every call site. In Spring, the factory becomes a `Map<String, PaymentMethod>` injected automatically, so adding a new provider is writing one class and nothing else.

The senior distinction to draw is between the simple parameterised factory, the formal Factory Method where subclasses override a creation step, and the Abstract Factory that produces whole families of related objects. At National Bank of India, centralising payment-method creation behind a factory is what lets the team onboard a new payment provider by adding one class, with zero churn in the checkout code that has already been tested and approved.

Remember one sentence: the Factory Method centralises object creation so callers ask for a type and the factory delivers the right product, keeping callers decoupled from concrete classes.
